title: Trump Administration Freezes $1 Billion in Medicaid Payments to California and Minnesota Over Fraud Claims
excerpt: Health Secretary RFK Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz accuse both states of suspected fraud, demanding documentation before funds are released.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump administration freezes over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota due to fraud claims.
  • California's frozen funds include $391 million for in-home services and $221 million for disputed immigration status claims.
  • Minnesota faces $3 million in frozen funds linked to deceased individuals and documentation gaps.
  • The freeze is part of a broader federal crackdown on healthcare fraud, charging 455 defendants for $6.5 billion in claims.
  • Healthcare advocates warn the fraud crackdown may deter eligible immigrants from seeking necessary care.

  • The Trump administration is deferring over $1 billion in federal Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota over suspected fraud and noncompliance
  • CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz cited $391 million in frozen California in-home services payments and $221 million tied to individuals with disputed immigration status
  • Both states must provide documentation proving their claims are legitimate before funds are released
  • The freeze is part of a broader federal healthcare fraud crackdown that has charged 455 defendants across 41 states for $6.5 billion in fraudulent claims

The Trump administration is pausing more than $1 billion in federal Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. accusing both Democratic-run states of suspected fraud and noncompliance, according to Reuters.

"If those states want that money they need to provide documentation that these payments are legitimate," Kennedy said at a news conference alongside CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz on Tuesday.

What the Freeze Covers

The payment suspension targets specific spending categories in both states. In California, $391 million of the frozen funds came from in-home supportive services, which include activities like driving patients to doctor appointments and assisting with basic daily tasks. Another $250 million involves claims tied to high-risk providers for which the state did not provide sufficient documentation.

Healthcare Fraud Crackdown Impact
›455 defendants charged across 41 states.
›$6.5 billion in fraudulent claims uncovered.
›102 durable medical equipment suppliers had payments suspended.
›725 billing privileges revoked from suppliers.

Of particular note for immigrant communities, CMS cited $221 million in associated claims involving individuals with what Oz described as "unsatisfactory immigration status."

"If it smells like fraud, we're not paying for it anymore."

— Dr. Mehmet Oz, CMS Administrator

In Minnesota, Oz said $3 million in federal funds were allocated to deceased individuals, with additional funds flagged for "documentation gaps." The state had already disenrolled nearly 3,000 healthcare providers from the program over its own fraud concerns.

States Push Back

California Governor Gavin Newsom dismissed the announcement as a "recycled political stunt," posting on X that the state was being targeted for political reasons rather than legitimate fraud concerns. He pointed out that neither Kennedy nor Oz provided evidence of actual fraud.

Minnesota Governor Tim Walz's office responded that the "Trump Administration is cutting more money in healthcare than they've prosecuted for fraud."

Oz countered that California's spending on the affected programs grew 24% over the past two federal fiscal years — twice the national average of 12%. "That doesn't make sense," he said.

Part of a Broader Crackdown

The Medicaid freeze is the latest in a series of payment suspensions targeting mostly Democratic-run states, part of what the White House has called an "unrelenting" war on healthcare fraud led by Vice President JD Vance, Kennedy, and Oz.

Last month, the Justice Department and HHS announced what they called the "greatest combined federal and state effort in combating health care fraud in history," spanning 57 federal districts across 41 states. The investigation uncovered more than $6.5 billion in fraudulent claims and brought charges against 455 defendants, including 90 licensed medical professionals.

CMS has also suspended payments to 102 durable medical equipment suppliers and revoked billing privileges for 725 others. Kennedy said the agency is now using AI and advanced analytics to identify suspicious spending patterns.

What It Means for Immigrant Healthcare Access

The inclusion of immigration-status-related claims in the California freeze has raised alarms among healthcare advocates. Rights groups have previously argued that Trump's fraud crackdown creates a "fearful environment" that deters eligible immigrants from seeking care.

The funds will remain frozen until both states can substantiate their claims from the previous quarter's audits. Kennedy said he was also expanding exclusion authority to CMS and HHS's Office of the Inspector General, allowing them to permanently ban "bad actors" from federal healthcare programs.

What to Watch

With Medicaid work requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill already projected to increase the uninsured population by more than 5 million by 2034 according to the Congressional Budget Office, the payment freeze adds another layer of uncertainty for states managing healthcare coverage for vulnerable populations, including immigrant communities that rely on Medicaid-funded services.
